limitations.text:
Limitations — Athlete Synthetic Patient Profile
Clinical Data (Synthea)
VO2 max and resting heart rate are single point-in-time Observations (2026-08-20), not a longitudinal fitness trend — no way to confirm consistency of the athletic profile over time
Active psychosocial findings (stress, social isolation, alcohol use, intimate partner abuse) coexist with elite fitness markers with no causal or contextual link modeled between them in the record
Single simulated life path — no alternative outcome represented
Wearable Donor Selection (LifeSnaps)
Race not matchable — attribute absent from source dataset
Age matchable only at a coarse threshold (<30 / ≥30), not exact age
Closest resting-heart-rate match to the subject (47.3 bpm vs. subject’s 47 bpm) was excluded solely for missing RMSSD — selection is data-availability-constrained, not purely criteria-optimal
Donor’s RMSSD is present on only 4 of 81 days — thin signal for HRV-based fitness comparison
Unmeasured confounders in the donor’s original recording period inherited without detection
Wearable Data Treatment
No modification applied in either direction — assumes the donor’s real baseline adequately represents both the subject’s fitness level and absence of disease, which is unverified
No representation of training-cycle variation (e.g., taper, peak, recovery weeks) an actual athlete’s wearable data would likely show
Data Integration
Clinical–wearable correspondence is constructed (sex-matched, fitness-proxy-ranked), not a unified measurement process
Daily data window (2026-06-17 to 2026-09-05) and hourly data window (ends 2026-08-31) are misaligned by several days due to sparser hourly recording in the original donor data
No downstream validation against clinical judgment or an established fitness/health classification method
No connection established between this profile and the companion profiles beyond shared population source

methodology.text:
A Synthetic Multi-Modal Athlete Patient Profile: Clinical and Wearable Data Integration
Subject: Shelton25 Danilo179 Graham902 (synthetic)
1. Clinical Data Generation
1.1 Population synthesis and candidate identification
The subject was drawn from the same Synthea-generated Massachusetts population used for the companion profiles. Candidate identification targeted patients with fitness-consistent physiological markers on record — specifically an Observation-level VO2 max measurement and resting heart rate — combined with the absence of chronic disease, to represent a physically high-functioning comparator distinct from both the disease and familial-risk profiles.
1.2 Subject validation
The selected subject’s record was confirmed against the following criteria:
VO2 max of 58.4 mL/kg/min, within the elite-endurance-athlete reference range
Resting heart rate of 47 bpm, consistent with trained cardiovascular adaptation
No active chronic disease — condition history limited to resolved routine/acute events and one minor musculoskeletal injury (ankle sprain, 2024)
A normal-range BMI trajectory across available longitudinal readings (20.1–24.3 kg/m² through adolescence, settling at 22.3)
The subject’s record additionally contains several currently active psychosocial findings (stress, social isolation, unhealthy alcohol use, intimate partner abuse victimization) documented as of the most recent encounter. These are reported factually in the accompanying Patient Profile document and were not used as selection or exclusion criteria for this comparator.
2. Wearable Data Source Selection
2.1 Target demographic and physiological profile
Male, date of birth 2003-07-04 (age 23 at time of wearable data collection), White. Physiological target: high cardiovascular fitness, consistent with the subject’s recorded VO2 max and resting heart rate.
2.2 Donor pool constraints
Filtering the LifeSnaps cohort to male participants in the <30 age bucket (the same constraint applied to the companion familial-risk profile, given identical demographic granularity limits) yielded 21 candidates.
2.3 Selection procedure
Selection criteria were oriented toward fitness rather than risk or neutrality: candidates were ranked for the lowest resting heart rate among those with non-missing heart rate variability (RMSSD) data, consistent with the RMSSD-completeness requirement applied across all three profiles in this series. The closest resting-heart-rate match to the subject’s own value (47.3 bpm) was excluded on this basis, as RMSSD was entirely absent from that candidate’s record.
Selected candidate: 621e30f467b776a240f22944 — resting heart rate 58.2 bpm (lowest among RMSSD-complete candidates), mean daily step count 9,446.8, RMSSD 51.0 ms (present on a subset of days), 81 days of daily- and hourly-resolution data.
3. Wearable Data Treatment
No disease-state physiological modification was applied. As with the familial-risk profile, the subject carries no active diagnosed condition, so the donor’s recorded values were used as-is. No fitness-amplifying modification was applied either — the donor’s real physiological profile (elevated activity, moderate-low resting heart rate) was judged a reasonable standalone representation of an athletic baseline without further adjustment.
4. Temporal Alignment
The wearable dataset’s native collection window (2021-11-03 to 2022-01-22) was shifted forward by a constant offset to terminate at the present date, consistent with the method applied to both companion profiles. The resulting daily-resolution window spans 2026-06-17 to 2026-09-05. The hourly-resolution data, sparser in the source recording, terminates several days earlier (2026-08-31) after the same offset is applied.
5. Data Files
athlete_profile_Shelton25_Graham902.json — clinical record (FHIR)
shelton_daily.csv — daily-resolution wearable data, 81 days, unmodified
shelton_hourly.csv — hourly-resolution wearable data, unmodified
